title: Verifier-Guided Prompting for Intent-to-Configuration Translation: A Preregistered NetOps Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory trial (N=150 synthetic intents; shared_initial_candidate semantics) to test whether constrained prompting combined with deterministic verifier-guided iterative feedback (generate→verify→repair, one allowed repair) materially increases verifier-level semantic correctness for natural-language → low-level network-configuration translation. Model: gpt-5-mini; verifier: deterministic_netops_validator_v5; adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Crucial execution semantics: for each intent a single initial model generation was shared across baseline and guarded conditions (shared_initial_candidate); the guarded pipeline could invoke at most one additional repair call if the verifier failed that initial candidate. Note: the preregistered constrained-only condition (B) was not executed and no confirmatory inference about B is reported. Results (confirmatory): baseline = 149/150 (99.333%), guarded = 150/150 (100.0%); paired absolute difference = 0.0066667 (0.67 percentage points); exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.02] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Only one guarded repair invocation occurred (1/150); median revision iterations = 0 (IQR = 0). Interpretation: on this preregistered synthetic corpus the guarded workflow yielded a numerically negligible and statistically non-significant improvement over an already near-ceiling baseline. We bound this empirical outcome to the provided synthetic corpus, single model, shared_initial_candidate execution semantics, and deterministic validator; we highlight a methodological lesson that pilot baseline calibration is necessary to avoid ceiling effects that invalidate preregistered power assumptions.

sections.introduction:
Natural-language intent interfaces seek to make network operations accessible by translating operator intent into concrete low-level configuration sequences. Prior work shows LLMs can produce configuration templates but frequently introduce syntactic or semantic errors that require downstream correction [1]. Deterministic, verifier-guided generate→verify→repair pipelines reduce such errors in infrastructure-as-code and configuration tasks in several prior studies [2], [3], and security analyses motivate runtime gating because textual claims can map to concrete actions in tool-augmented agent pipelines [4], [5].

Research question. After a fresh literature grounding we preregistered the following confirmatory question: Does constrained prompting (structured templates + explicit semantic slots) combined with deterministic verifier-guided iterative feedback materially increase verifier-level semantic correctness of NL→configuration translation compared to an unconstrained baseline under a paired design? The study was preregistered (study_cand_2026_b2_v1) and frozen before observing outcomes.

Contributions. (1) A preregistered paired confirmatory design that measures machine-checkable verifier pass/fail as the principal outcome. (2) A complete archived execution on N=150 paired tasks using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic NetOps validator under shared_initial_candidate semantics. (3) An artifact-grounded empirical result showing a negligible marginal numeric benefit of a single-repair guarded pipeline on the supplied synthetic corpus, and a methodological recommendation (pilot baseline calibration) for future preregistered NetOps trials.
sections.related_work: Three research strands guided the design. First, intent-to-configuration and NL→formal-spec evaluations report modest semantic-correctness in many benchmarks and emphasize the difficulty of producing verifier-sound formalizations from free text [1]. Second, verifier-aware generation and iterative repair (generate→verify→repair) improve correctness for infrastructure artifacts when paired with deterministic or policy-guided verifiers [2], [3]. Third, security analyses demonstrate that agentic LLM pipelines can convert false textual claims into concrete actions and motivate runtime gating, audit trails, and tool-call policies [4], [5]. Finally, formal network-verification tools (e.g., NetKAT descendants and fast symbolic verifiers) offer deterministic oracles for reachability, isolation, and policy checks and are appropriate for verifier-level outcome measurement [6]. This study situates a preregistered paired trial at the intersection of these strands and uses deterministic verifier pass/fail as the confirmatory endpoint.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design: The study was preregistered as study_cand_2026_b2_v1 and frozen prior to observing outcomes (preregistration SHA-256 = aea996afce45e3798345f6e32ae6c347456f103ecdb84fc36e27bb486a329399). The confirmatory design is a paired binary comparison between (A) baseline free-text prompting and (C) constrained-template prompting plus deterministic verifier-guided single-repair (guarded). A constrained-only condition (B) was preregistered conceptually but was not executed in the confirmatory run; no confirmatory statistics for B are reported.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics (explicit). For each intent exactly one initial model generation was produced and that same sampled initial candidate was used for both the baseline and guarded evaluations; the guarded pipeline was permitted at most one additional repair call if and only if the deterministic verifier failed the initial candidate. This means the observed baseline rate measures initial-candidate validity, and the guarded vs baseline contrast isolates the marginal effect of the single allowed repair given that common initial generation. The execution manifest and analysis artifacts record this semantics and the provider-call audit (see analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json in the archived bundle).

Population, sampling, and tasks: Confirmatory sample N=150 distinct synthetic intents programmatically generated (balanced across four intent families as described in the preregistration) and topologies restricted to verifier-capable toy-to-small networks. Inclusion/exclusion: ambiguity detection and parser/verifier-coverage exclusion rules were applied deterministically prior to model calls; no confirmatory exclusions occurred during this run.

Models, tools, and budgets: declared model = gpt-5-mini; deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; adapter family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Execution budget: at most one initial model call per intent and at most one repair call per intent (planned episodes = 300; maximum_model_calls = 300). Recorded execution totals: completed episodes = 300; model_calls_used = 151; repair-stage invocations observed = 1.

Primary estimand and analysis (pre-registered): paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; primary test = exact McNemar two-sided; 95% bootstrap percentile CI with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Missingness plan: primary analysis uses complete pairs (complete_pair_primary); no missing pairs occurred. All analysis code and verdict logs are archived; analysis artifacts identify the confirmatory result and show contingency counts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/condition_summary.csv).

Artifact labeling note and reconciliation. The preregistration text enumerated hypotheses (H1: constrained vs baseline; H2: guarded vs constrained), but the execution/analysis preserved a single registered primary_estimand corresponding to guarded vs baseline (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline). The archived analysis objects encode the executed confirmatory contrast under hypothesis_id = "H1" in the analysis output; deterministic_reconciliation.json and analysis/results.json consistently document that this hypothesis_id maps to guarded vs baseline in the executed run. We explicitly report the executed contrast (guarded vs baseline) and note that the preregistered textual hypothesis labels differ from the analysis-file hypothesis_id mapping; this is a documentation alignment clarified here and in the archived bundle.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and raw counts: planned paired episodes = 300; completed_episode_count = 300; complete_pair_count = 150; model_calls_used = 151; repair-stage invocations observed = 1. Paired contingency (guarded × baseline): n_11 = 149 (both-pass), n_10 = 1 (guarded-only-pass), n_01 = 0 (baseline-only-pass), n_00 = 0 (both-fail). Per-condition success rates: baseline_success_count = 149/150 = 0.9933333333333333; guarded_success_count = 150/150 = 1.0. Estimated paired absolute difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00666666666666671 (≈0.67 percentage points).

Statistical results (pre-registered test): exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the difference = [0.00, 0.02] (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Missingness/exclusions/contamination: none observed; deterministic reconciliation and the analysis missingness_summary.csv show zero excluded or failed episodes.

Repair diagnostics: only one guarded repair invocation occurred (1/150); median revision iterations in guarded episodes = 0 (IQR = 0). Operational interpretation of numbers given shared_initial_candidate semantics: since the same initial sampled candidate was used for both conditions, the baseline rate (149/150) reflects the validity of that initial candidate; the guarded pipeline had only a single observable opportunity to improve results and did so once.

Result summary: on the preregistered synthetic corpus and under the shared_initial_candidate execution semantics, constrained prompting plus a single verifier-guided repair produced a numerically small (0.67 pp) and statistically non-significant improvement over a near-ceiling baseline.
sections.discussion:
Null vs ceiling interpretation. The near-ceiling baseline (149/150 initial-candidate successes) produced a ceiling effect that invalidated the preregistered power assumptions (the planned detectable absolute effect was 15 percentage points). As a result, the confirmatory contrast had little room to observe improvement: only a single repair invocation occurred and the paired difference was negligible. This does not contradict prior evidence that verifier-guided repair can produce larger gains when baselines are weaker or tasks are more diverse [2], [3].

Methodological recommendation. Future preregistered LLM-for-NetOps confirmatory trials should include a small pilot baseline-calibration step to estimate initial-candidate competence and adjust sample size or task difficulty to avoid ceiling effects. Doing so preserves the statistical information content of the planned contrast and aligns power assumptions with observed baseline competence.

Operational implication. When base-model initial-candidate correctness is already near 100% for representative tasks, single-repair guarded pipelines yield marginal numeric returns but still provide explicit gating points, auditable decision records, and integration affordances for human-in-the-loop policies.

Threats to validity. Internal: paired shared_initial_candidate semantics mean the contrast isolates the marginal repair effect given a shared initial sample; different generation semantics (independent per-condition sampling) or a larger repair budget could change outcomes. Construct: verifier pass/fail is a machine-checkable proxy for semantic correctness but depends on verifier coverage and mapping correctness. External: single-model constraint (gpt-5-mini), synthetic corpus limited to verifier-capable toy-to-small topologies (4–32 nodes), and single-repair budget limit generalizability to production WANs, heterogeneous device CLIs, and adversarial intents. Conclusion validity: planned power assumed a much larger baseline deficit than observed; the ceiling effect reduced sensitivity to practical gains. All these threats are documented in the preregistration and in the archived artifact bundle.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired confirmatory trial comparing baseline free-text prompting to a constrained-template plus deterministic-verifier single-repair guarded workflow under shared_initial_candidate semantics using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic NetOps validator. On the archived synthetic corpus the guarded workflow increased verifier pass rate from 149/150 to 150/150 (0.67 percentage points), a numerically tiny and statistically non-significant change (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.02]). The principal scientific outcome is methodological: preregistered LLM-for-NetOps trials must pilot and calibrate baseline competence to avoid ceiling effects that render planned contrasts uninformative. Technically, these results bound the benefit of a single-repair guarded pipeline on the supplied synthetic corpus, single model, and deterministic validator; they do not contradict prior reports that verifier guidance can materially help in more challenging settings.

limitations: Single-model constraint: experiments used only gpt-5-mini; results do not generalize across models or sizes.

Synthetic corpus and scale: tasks were programmatically generated and limited to verifier-capable toy-to-small topologies (4–32 nodes); external validity to production WANs and heterogeneous vendor CLIs is untested.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and execution contract limited repair budget to at most one guarded repair call per intent; different generation semantics or multiple-repair budgets may yield different outcomes.

Ceiling effect and preregistration mismatch: baseline correctness was far higher than the pilot assumptions used for power calculations (planned detectable effect = 15 percentage points), reducing the trial's ability to demonstrate benefit and illustrating sensitivity to baseline calibration.

Verifier coverage and specification translation: the study measures verifier pass/fail on the preregistered invariants but does not claim full operational safety guarantees beyond the deterministic validator's modeled properties.

Security and adversarial robustness: the experiment did not evaluate adversarial prompt-injection or adversary-driven intents; separate targeted studies are required to assess claim-to-action vulnerabilities in agentic NetOps workflows.
